fact_claims.verbatim: 8.1 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units company-wide
4 incidents not reported to a regulator
flagship model’s 55 °C sustained-heat test failure rate was 3.9%
its thermal incident rate was 9.9 per 100,000 installed units
81% of our installed units support remote emergency shut-off
Adding built-in fire suppression costs about $67 per unit

S1_incident_reporting.quote: Manufacturers must report every thermal incident involving overheating, smoke, fire, injury, or property damage to the relevant regulator within 72 hours of becoming aware of it, including incidents initially reported by customers or installers. Manufacturers must notify affected customers within 5 days when an incident indicates a credible safety risk, and provide updates when material facts change. Reports must not be withheld because an investigation is ongoing; a manufacturer may supplement them later.

S2_thermal_testing.quote: Each model must undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C before sale and after a material design or manufacturing change, using a regulator-approved protocol and representative sample. The maximum permitted failure rate is 5% of tested units per model. A model exceeding 5% must promptly undergo corrective review and submit a mitigation plan and implementation schedule to regulators. Exceeding the limit alone does not automatically require sales suspension; regulators may impose proportionate restrictions, including suspension, based on the test results, incident evidence, and adequacy of the mitigation plan. Manufacturers must submit per-model results, sample sizes, and test methods to regulators and provide the results for a model to customers who buy that model, including prospective customers before purchase. Results need not be publicly disclosed beyond those recipients.

S3_remote_shutoff.quote: New units must support secure remote emergency shut-off, with appropriate protections against unauthorized activation and a local means of safe operation. For units already installed, manufacturers must provide a retrofit or equivalent compliant capability within 6 years of this standard’s effective date. Where retrofit is impracticable, the manufacturer must document the reason and provide customers with an alternative mitigation plan.

S4_fire_suppression.quote: New units must include built-in fire suppression beginning 36 months after this standard’s adoption. The suppression system must be appropriate to the battery chemistry and installation, and must not create additional hazards during normal use, maintenance, or emergency response.

S5_customer_disclosure.quote: A manufacturer must initiate a recall when any model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a year. The recall must promptly protect affected customers and may use an appropriate remedy such as repair, retrofit, replacement, or refund; it does not by itself require a permanent market ban. Regulators may require an earlier recall or other corrective action when the evidence indicates an imminent or serious risk. Recall notices must explain the hazard, affected units, and remedy, and be sent promptly to affected customers and regulators.

document.section_notes: All four red lines are respected: S2 per-model results go to purchasers and regulators but need not be published (NW-1, HC-1); S3 retrofit is 6 years (NW-2); S4 built-in suppression starts at 36 months (HC-2). S1 is broadly safe (all incidents, 72h/3-day reporting, 5-day customer notice, reporting during investigation), and S5 keeps a mandatory numeric 8/100k recall trigger with 5-day notices, which directly bites Halcyon's Ember 8 (9.9/100k) and is the main anti-Halcyon feature. S2's weak point is that exceeding the 5% limit never automatically stops sales (only corrective review plus regulator discretion), which protects Northwind's Hearth 10 (6.2% failure); S3's new-unit shut-off obligation has no stated deadline (read as from adoption).
